newsitem.title: USA: High-grade US corporate bonds rise as junk wanders.
newsitem.headline: High-grade US corporate bonds rise as junk wanders.

text.p: Investment-grade U.S. corporate bond prices continued to strengthen on Tuesday, lifted by solid buying from institutional investors, according to high-grade traders.

Conversely, traders described the high-yield market as slow and sloppy. "Prices in the (junk) market have been ill-defined. It's like the first day of school - no one knows what is going on," said one trader.
In the high-grade market, the cable sector registered the most gains. Long-term bonds of Tele-Communications Inc tightened by 15-20 basis points on the day, said one trader.
Viacom Inc long-term debt rose by five to seven basis points as well, traders said.

Marion Boucher Soper, telecommunications and media high-grade debt analyst at Bear Stearns & Co Inc, said Tuesday's gains were the result of continued improvements in investor sentiment about cable companies, rather than any new financial development in the sector.

Boucher Soper said Viacom bonds, which have been trading at cheap levels recently, could tighten by another 20 basis points if the company carries out its plans to reduce its debt level in the first half of 1997.

"In the case of TCI, it's more complicated. They will be meeting with Standard & Poor's over the next month and no one has any sense of the outcome. If it's positive, the bonds could tighten by 30-40 basis points. If it's negative, the same could happen in the opposite direction," she said.
Boucher Souper was referring to the rating agency's upcoming decision on whether to downgrade TCI's credit rating due to its high debt levels and declining cash flow.
In the junk market, prices in the supermarket sector weakened substantially, as prices in the overall market were unchanged to slightly lower.
Penn Traffic Inc bonds fell several points in trading, but ended the day at roughly the same levels. The company recently reported a drop in same store sales of 8.5 percent for December.
Elsewhere, Moody's Investors Service downgraded Hills Stores Co senior notes due 2003 to B2 from B1.

"The downgrade reflects eroding operating profit margins, decling cash flow from operations, limited sources of liquidity aside from (a) bank facility and increased competition in its markets," said Moody's of the Canton, Massachusetts-based department store chain.

The move sent prices on the bonds spiraling down to 69 from their opening levels of 74, traders said. By the end of the day, however, the bonds made back most of their losses, closing at 73, they noted.
In the Treasury market, concerns about stronger economic growth pushed the price of the 30-year benchmark Treasury down 7/32 to 96-9/32. The yield rose to 6.79 percent.
